Chapter 9—Sustaining the Coaching Habit: Dealing with Setbacks and Staying the Course.
Building and keeping up the coaching habit really is a journey. You’ll notice progress, hit a few bumps, and keep learning along the way. Even the most dedicated leaders sometimes slip back into old routines—especially when things get hectic or stressful. The trick? Meet those moments with a little self-compassion and a growth mindset.
Think about it this way: setbacks aren’t failures—they’re just chances to reflect and reset. If you catch yourself giving advice instead of asking thoughtful questions, don’t be too hard on yourself. Just pause, recognize what happened, and gently steer yourself back to that coaching approach. Each small course correction you make actually strengthens your habit and builds your resilience over time.
So, how do you keep the coaching habit alive? Here are a few things that really help:
First, make it a routine to reflect. Set aside a little time each week to look back at your recent conversations—where did your curiosity shine, and where could you dig a little deeper next time? Next, ask for feedback. Invite your colleagues or team members to share what it felt like to be coached by you. Listen closely for ways you can keep improving.
Don’t forget to celebrate progress. Notice even the small shifts in how you show up or the outcomes you see. And every now and then, reconnect with your purpose. Remind yourself why coaching matters—not just for you, but for your team and your whole organization.
Here’s a simple analogy that might help: think of the coaching habit like tending a garden. Some days, you’ll see growth and feel rewarded. Other days, it’s all about patience and steady care. The important thing is to keep showing up, nurturing your habit, and trusting that your effort will pay off.
Over time, leaders who stick with the coaching approach find it becomes second nature—a real part of who they are. They feel less stressed, more satisfied, and build stronger, more meaningful connections with their teams. And maybe best of all, they help create a culture where everyone gets the chance to learn, grow, and truly thrive.
